verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: message #1 reports field data loss with a repro, and the change makes vacuumlo delete less. The two surviving objections are fixable design points. maintenance-fit-1 asks to split the domain fix from composite and array support, and maintenance-fit-2 asks for a warning on type kinds vacuumlo still cannot search. Neither stops review at level 2.

brief.title: Teach vacuumlo to find large object references in domains and composite types
brief.problem: vacuumlo only scans columns whose type is named oid or lo, so it treats large objects referenced from a domain over oid or lo as orphaned and deletes them. The docs mention this, but users still lose data during routine maintenance. vacuumlo gives no warning, and -n lists these objects as removable without saying why.
brief.proposed_design: Patch 0001 makes vacuumlo search the catalog recursively for oid or lo inside domains, including domains over domains, composite types and arrays. The catalog query returns a matching search expression for each column, which vacuumlo then uses in its delete statement. Patch 0002 documents the data loss risk for column types vacuumlo does not recognize and points users to the lo extension.
user_visible_surface: vacuumlo now keeps large objects referenced from domain, composite and array columns that it used to remove.
vacuumlo documentation gains a data loss warning for column types it does not recognize, such as text.
author_claims: Domains over base types are common, and users have hit this data loss in the field.
Everything vacuumlo needs is in the catalog, so it can cover all ways a column can hold an oid or lo.
The change may help only somewhat, because some users store large object references in text or other types.
Most users should use lo_manage() or custom triggers from the lo extension, which would make vacuumlo a cleanup tool for legacy schemas.
brief.thread_state: Nathan Bossart sent v1 for domains, and Sami Imseih sent v2, which also covers composite and array types and adds docs. No one has reviewed v2 on the visible thread, and the entry has moved through 4 CommitFests in Needs review.
unclear: Whether v2 adds the tests Nathan asked for, since the touched files are not listed.
Whether vacuumlo warns about columns it still skips, which message #1 suggested.
How the deeper scan and the more complex delete statements affect run time on large databases.
Whether the change will be back-patched, given that it fixes a data loss bug.
Why commit 64c604898e chose to document domains instead of handling them; the thread found no reason.

objections.title: Domain fix and composite/array expansion are bundled in one patch
objections.failure_scenario: A user on a released branch keeps a domain over oid. vacuumlo deletes those large objects, and v2 can only reach that user if a committer agrees to back-patch per-column delete expressions for composites and arrays. If no committer will take that on, the domain fix waits as well. Meanwhile the data loss continues on every supported branch.
objections.argument: v1 (message #4) was a small recursive query over typbasetype, which is a plausible back-patch candidate for a data loss bug. v2 (message #7) merges that fix with generated search expressions for composite and array types in one patch, 0001. Nobody has reviewed v2 on the visible thread across 4 CommitFests. The larger change is harder to review, test and back-patch, and few committers work on vacuumlo (message #2).
objections.author_must_show: Can the domain-over-oid fix be split out as a standalone first patch suitable for back-patching, with composite and array support in a separate patch?

critic.reasoning: Message #7 puts domain, composite and array handling in one patch, 0001, and the visible thread has no review of v2. The back-patch part is speculative because the behavior is documented, but the request to split the patch stands without it.

objections.title: Type kinds that are not covered are still skipped silently
objections.failure_scenario: A user stores large object OIDs in a range or multirange over oid, or in a container kind added in a later release. vacuumlo removes those objects without a message. The user finds out when lo_get() fails.
objections.argument: Message #5 says the approach can "cover all potential ways an OID or LO can be used". The brief lists only domains, composites and arrays, so ranges and multiranges appear to be left out. A future container kind would also be missed, and nothing would fail loudly when that happens. Message #1 asked for a warning about skipped columns, and the brief does not say v2 adds one. Without that warning, coverage depends on someone remembering to update vacuumlo.
objections.author_must_show: Does vacuumlo detect columns where oid or lo is nested in a type kind it cannot search, and warn about them, so that a missing case does not cause silent deletion?

critic.reasoning: Postgres allows a range over oid, and the material lists only domains, composites and arrays. The silent skip exists today and 0002 documents the risk, but the warning that message #1 suggested is not shown in v2.

refuted.title: Composite and array coverage goes beyond the demand that was reported
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer reviewing v2 has to verify generated delete expressions for nested composite types and arrays inside domains. No user in the thread has reported losing a large object referenced from a composite or array column, so this extra SQL generation must be maintained and reviewed for a case nobody has asked about.
refuted.argument: The field report in message #1 and its repro cover only a domain over oid. Message #4 shows that the domain case needs only a recursive query. Message #5 extends the scope to composite types and oid[] because they are "detectable from the catalog", and it also doubts that this "moves the needle". A committer would likely accept the domain fix on the evidence shown and ask for separate evidence before taking on the composite and array part.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users store large object references in composite or array columns, and would a domain-only patch leave them losing data today?

critic.reasoning: The scenario describes review effort, which is not a failure, and the cost falls only on vacuumlo. Composite and array columns have the same silent deletion, Nathan Bossart called the extension "worth exploring" in message #6, and maintenance-fit-1 covers the split.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: vacuumlo, often run as superuser, builds delete statements from type and attribute names read from the catalog.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The patch fixes data loss on released branches, and the thread does not settle whether it is back-patched.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: vacuumlo gains a recursive catalog query and generated per-column search expressions that must follow new type kinds.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Can the domain fix be a standalone first patch, with composite and array support in a second patch?
Does vacuumlo warn when a column nests oid or lo in a type kind it cannot search, such as a range or multirange?
Is the domain fix proposed for back-patching, given that the current behavior is documented?
Does the recursive catalog query run when a new vacuumlo connects to an older supported server?
How much longer does vacuumlo run on a database with many tables once it uses the deeper scan and the generated delete expressions?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows contrib client tools and the type catalog. Nathan Bossart sent v1 and is listed as reviewer, but the material does not show his role, and no one has reviewed v2.
committability.liability: The owner signs for vacuumlo's delete decisions: a wrong generated search expression deletes referenced large objects, and that loss is irreversible. The type coverage must be kept current as new type kinds appear.
committability.author_follow_up: Sami Imseih sent v2 and moved the entry to the next CommitFest twice, most recently on 2026-11-10.

priority.reason: The patch fixes irreversible data loss for vacuumlo users who keep large object references in domain columns, and the cost falls only on vacuumlo. Review cost is medium because no code was read and v2 generates SQL; splitting out the domain fix would lower it.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check that the generated expressions quote identifiers and cover nested cases correctly, or whether v2 adds tests. Messages #4 to #7 were not shown, so the scope of v2 rests on the brief.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: vacuumlo: report the number of large objects going to be removed
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes vacuumlo report how many large objects it will remove and, in a second part, the percentage removed so far. Version 2 takes the count from PQcmdTuples() instead of a separate SELECT count(*) on the temp table.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers did not object to the idea. The last review round left open requests: Michael Paquier asked for raw deleted and to-delete counts next to the percentage, and Daniel Verite asked for unsigned long counters because the number of large objects can exceed 2^31. Version 2 also had wrong indentation. The visible messages show no reply or new version from the author after these comments.

precedents_retrieved.title: vacuumlo: add test to vacuumlo for test coverage
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a TAP test for vacuumlo to raise its test coverage. The test runs vacuumlo in verbose dry-run mode against one database.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not reply to review comments or post a new version, so the entry was returned with feedback. Daniel Gustafsson asked for more scenarios, such as a database that does not exist or one with no large objects, and asked the test to use run_command(). Ian Lawrence Barwick noted that the test was not added to meson.build.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There has been no updates on this thread for some time, so this has
been switched as Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: improve large object handling in pg_upgrade
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal changes pg_upgrade so it can handle clusters with hundreds of millions of large objects. pg_restore would restore large objects in batched transactions, and new pg_upgrade options would pass arbitrary pg_dump/pg_restore options through.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After the XID problem was largely addressed by 74cf7d46a, Jacob Champion objected that a --dump-options pass-through lets users give pg_upgrade flags such as --exclude-schema that could break the new cluster. Nathan Bossart agreed and said it was not yet clear how to proceed. The thread then went quiet for more than four weeks, and Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
What I'm
questioning is the addition of --dump-options to make use of that fix
from pg_upgrade, since it also lets the user do "exciting" new things
like --exclude-schema and --include-foreign-data and so on.

precedents_retrieved.title: Identifying user-created objects
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a SQL function pg_is_user_object() that returns true when an object's OID is at or above FirstNormalObjectId, so users can tell objects created after initdb from built-in ones. The stated aim was a security check, for PCI DSS 2.2.5, that no malicious functions exist in pg_catalog.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Kyotaro Horiguchi argued that an OID-based check does not serve the security purpose: anyone able to install a malicious function can also give it a low OID, and built-in functions such as pg_read_file are not safe just because they are built in. The author agreed a method that does not rely on OIDs would be better. Later the patch stopped compiling because of an OID collision in pg_proc.dat, no new version came, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
In the first place, if you assume that someone may install malicious
functions in the server after beginning operation, distinction by OID
doesn't work at all because who can illegally install a malicious
function also be able to modify its OID with quite low odds.

precedents_retrieved.title: Incorrect handling of OOM in WAL replay leading to data loss
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds an error code (none, out-of-memory, invalid data) to the xlogreader error state, so callers can tell an OOM apart from an invalid record. The startup process then retries the record on OOM during crash recovery, so recovery does not end early and lose data.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it. Commit 6b18b3fe2c2f had already made xlogreader.c fail harder on OOM, which leaves HEAD correct in the OOM cases. The patch set would have reverted that and made the xlogreader error layers more complicated, and nobody showed interest after a further commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Moving relation extension locks out of heavyweight lock manager
precedents_retrieved.summary: Move relation extension locks out of the heavyweight lock manager into a separate lightweight mechanism in shared memory, because these locks need neither multiple lock modes nor deadlock detection. The first draft used a shared hash table of LWLocks; later versions used a fixed-size array of lock entries (N_RELEXTLOCK_ENTS) indexed by a hash of the relation, so a backend can find and reuse a lock's address without a mapping lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks showed regressions of up to 25% when different relations hashed to the same lock entry. Andres Freund was not convinced that such false collisions would be rare, citing partitioning and the birthday paradox, and doubted that a larger array would fix it. Robert Haas argued that removing collisions would require a mapping lock and extra atomic operations on every extension, and the question was not resolved. The thread then went quiet, and Michael Paquier returned the entry because it seemed hard to reach a committable state for v11.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Also, birthday paradoxon and all that make collisions not that unlikely. And you really don't need a 16 way conflict to feel pain, you'll imo feel it earlier.

precedents_retrieved.title: Warning for Datatype mismatch between subscriber table and publisher table for logical replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes logical replication emit a warning when a subscriber table column has a different data type from the matching publisher column. The goal is to show type mismatches early so users can debug replication problems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not revise the patch after review, and it had not passed CI since about mid March, so the CF entry was closed. Ashutosh Bapat had asked for the unrelated file renames to be removed. He also noted that the code maps columns by position, and that it compares type OIDs and names on the subscriber without using the remote type cache.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since this has not been fixed, and the patch has not passed CI since at least
mid March, I'll close this CF entry.

precedents_retrieved.title: SimpleLruTruncate() mutual exclusion (data loss from lack thereof)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch serializes SLRU truncation so that only one backend at a time runs vac_truncate_clog() and asyncQueueAdvanceTail() per cluster, and vac_update_datfrozenxid() per database. This closes a race in which two concurrent truncations can unlink a pg_xact segment that a backend has just recreated, which loses data.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tom Lane questioned whether serialization fixes the race and wanted to keep concurrent truncation directory scans, and Noah Misch answered with a concrete event sequence. Dmitry Dolgov could not reproduce the bug with the posted script and measured only a small latency increase, and the thread ends there with no withdrawal message.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found in the list. Message #2 reports that commit 64c604898e and its thread only documented the domain limitation and gave no reason against resolving domains, so no earlier rejection reason applies here.

From the standards and compatibility angle I found no objection that would hold. The patch adds no syntax, no GUC, no catalog object and no dump state. The behaviour change goes in the safe direction: vacuumlo keeps large objects it used to delete, so no script loses data after the upgrade. I could not check four things without the code. First, whether the recursive catalog query still runs when a new vacuumlo connects to an older server. Second, whether the docs drop the sentence 'domains over them are not considered'. Third, whether range types over oid or lo are covered or listed as not handled. Fourth, whether the change is back-patched.

vacuumlo is a client program that reads pg_type and pg_attribute and calls lo_unlink through ordinary SQL. The patches change no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol message or server ABI, so this angle finds no persistent or cross-node state to object to.

The proposal does not change who may run vacuumlo or what it may delete; it only makes vacuumlo keep more large objects, which lowers data loss risk. Reading domain, composite and array columns runs no user-defined code, so a superuser-run vacuumlo gains no new escalation path. Without the code I could not check that generated expressions quote type and attribute names and schema-qualify any functions they call.
The idea fits contrib and fixes data loss. The added cost falls only on vacuumlo runs over schemas that use these types, so the objections concern patch shape and coverage.

No existing feature does this job. The lo extension's lo_manage() prevents new orphans but cannot stop vacuumlo from deleting objects referenced from domain, composite or array columns, and vacuumlo has no option to name extra columns. The proposal fixes an existing contrib tool and adds no second mechanism.

Demand for the domain case is real: message #1 reports field data loss and includes a repro, and two committers-level participants agree it is worth fixing. The only objection is about the extra scope beyond domains.
